questions.question: What does `itertools.chain(a, b)` do?
options: Merges two iterables into one iterator without creating an intermediate combined list.
Raises an error if the two iterables have different lengths.
Sorts the combined result automatically.
Only works with lists, not other iterables.
questions.explanation: itertools.chain lazily iterates over each iterable in sequence, producing a single iterator without ever building a new combined list — memory-efficient for large sequences.

questions.question: Why must a sequence be sorted by key before using `itertools.groupby` on it?
options: groupby only works on sorted numbers.
groupby only groups consecutive items sharing a key, so unsorted input produces multiple small groups instead of one full group per key.
groupby requires alphabetical order specifically.
groupby modifies the list in place, which requires pre-sorting.
questions.explanation: itertools.groupby doesn't scan ahead to find all matching items — it only groups runs of consecutive equal keys, so unsorted input silently produces multiple separate groups for the same key value.

questions.question: What does `Counter(votes).most_common(2)` return?
options: The 2 least common items.
The total count of all items combined.
A list of the 2 (item, count) pairs with the highest counts, in descending order.
A set containing the 2 most common items.
questions.explanation: most_common(n) returns a list of (element, count) tuples ordered from most frequent to least, truncated to n entries.

questions.question: What problem does `collections.defaultdict` solve compared to a plain dict?
options: It automatically sorts keys.
It makes dicts immutable.
It removes duplicate keys automatically.
It supplies a default value for a missing key instead of raising KeyError.
questions.explanation: defaultdict(list) (or any factory) calls the factory to create a value the first time a key is accessed, avoiding a manual 'if key not in dict' check before appending.

questions.question: What does `functools.lru_cache` do to a function?
options: Makes the function's arguments optional.
Converts the function into a class.
Caches return values by argument so repeated calls with the same arguments skip re-computing the result.
Limits how many times the function can be called in total.
questions.explanation: lru_cache memoizes results keyed by the function's arguments; calling it again with the same arguments returns the cached value instantly instead of re-running the function body.

questions.question: What does `functools.partial(power, exponent=2)` create?
options: A new callable identical to power but with exponent already fixed at 2, needing only the remaining argument(s).
A copy of power that runs twice as fast.
A decorator that validates power's arguments.
An error, since partial only works with positional arguments.
questions.explanation: functools.partial pre-fills one or more arguments of a callable, returning a new callable that only needs the rest — calling the result with just the base is equivalent to power(base, exponent=2).

questions.question: What does the `@dataclass` decorator generate for you automatically?
options: Only a custom __str__ method.
A database table matching the class.
Type coercion that converts values to the annotated type at runtime.
__init__, __repr__, and __eq__ based on the declared fields, without writing them by hand.
questions.explanation: @dataclass writes __init__ (with field defaults), __repr__ (readable printing), and __eq__ (field-by-field comparison) for you — but it does NOT enforce or coerce the annotated types at runtime; those remain just hints.

questions.question: In a dataclass, what does `field(default_factory=list)` do that `default=[]` cannot?
options: Nothing — they behave identically.
Makes the field read-only.
Creates a NEW empty list for each instance, avoiding the mutable-default bug where every instance would share the same list.
Converts the field to a tuple.
questions.explanation: A plain default=[] would be one single list object shared by every instance (the same mutable-default trap as function arguments); default_factory=list calls list() fresh for each new instance instead.

questions.question: When does `__post_init__` run in a dataclass?
options: Before __init__ assigns any fields.
Automatically, immediately after __init__ has assigned all the declared fields.
Only when the object is printed.
It never runs unless called manually.
questions.explanation: __post_init__ is called automatically by the generated __init__ right after all declared fields are assigned, making it the right place to compute derived values from those fields.

questions.question: When is it better to write your own loop instead of reaching for itertools/functools/collections?
options: Always — the standard library should never be used for this kind of task.
When the stdlib tool's specific behavior (e.g. groupby's consecutive-only grouping, or an unbounded cache) would be less clear or correct than a straightforward loop for your case.
Never — stdlib tools are always faster.
Only when working with strings.
questions.explanation: The standard library tools are optimized and well-tested, but choosing them without understanding their edge cases (unsorted groupby, unbounded lru_cache) can introduce subtle bugs — a plain loop is sometimes clearer and just as correct for simple cases.
